summary:
Minoan Pulse is an offline crew-health assistant for long-duration missions, where the link to Earth is delayed or lost. It runs entirely on a laptop with no internet connection.

It monitors cabin CO2, potable-water pH and crew vital signs in real time. A deterministic rule engine, based on NASA-STD-3001 limits, decides whether a reading is out of range. A local AI model (Llama 3.2 3B) explains each alert, using only NASA documents retrieved from an offline library, and every recommended check cites its NASA source. Unsupported suggestions are removed automatically.

Before raising an alarm, the system asks whether the reading can be trusted. Machine-learning models detect sensor faults, such as a loose ECG electrode, so they do not cause false alarms. A 3D body twin with a smart pressure sleeve lets astronauts show exactly where it hurts. Per-astronaut baselines avoid alarms that are only "abnormal for the average person".

When the onboard library has no procedure, or the crew asks a medical question, Minoan Pulse writes a structured report for the flight surgeon. The report waits in a queue that survives communication blackouts and is delivered automatically when the link returns.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Minoan Pulse is a desktop "mission control" for crew health, built as one window with four tabs:

  1. Monitoring – live cabin CO2, water pH and heart rate, with NASA limits drawn on every chart and a 3D Station View built on NASA's ISS model. A rule engine checks every reading: it flags missing timestamps, wrong units, impossible values and stuck sensors, and it computes the 1-hour CO2 average from NASA-STD-3001 V2 6004. Alerts are explained by a local LLM with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over NASA technical briefs.
  2. Crew Health – a two-layer machine-learning console. Layer 1 (random forest) audits each data frame for sensor faults, such as a loose garment ECG, a cold drink passing a core-temperature capsule, a local CO2 pocket the wall sensor misses, or a radiation bit-flip. Layer 2 estimates risks only from data that passed the audit, and each risk comes with a per-sample explanation.
  3. Body Twin – a 3D astronaut with 12 body zones and a 48-sensor smart sleeve, inspired by the CSA Bio-Monitor. Pressing the sore spot for 2 seconds reports pain. A broken sensor is shown in grey, never as an alarm.
  4. Crew – a profile, personal baselines and a health log for each astronaut. The same heart rate can be normal for one person and unusual for another. Cycle-aware rules prevent false alarms during the luteal phase. A smartwatch preview vibrates only for critical events, and non-urgent findings wait for the next break in the schedule.

SAFETY BY DESIGN

  • The AI never decides whether a value is dangerous: code does, using NASA limits.
  • The AI may cite only documents that were actually retrieved, because the JSON schema restricts its source IDs.
  • Every recommended check must share at least 60% of its content words with its cited source, or it is dropped.
  • With no matching document, it says "no onboard procedure" and escalates. It never diagnoses or suggests medication.
  • Escalations go to an outbox: SQLite with exponential backoff and a retry when the link returns. Nothing is lost during loss of signal.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Pydantic, scikit-learn, pandas, Streamlit), JavaScript (three.js, Chart.js, Google model-viewer, Astro UX Design System), Node.js, SQLite, Ollama with Llama 3.2 3B and nomic-embed-text, faster-whisper (offline speech-to-text) and Piper (offline text-to-speech), and pywebview for the desktop window. 148 automated tests.

IMPACT

NASA notes that deep-space crews will need Earth-independent medical operations. Minoan Pulse shows how crews could act on trusted, sourced information during communication gaps, while avoiding false alarms from faulty sensors.

LIMITATIONS

All data is simulated. Heart-rate thresholds and the cycle-phase adjustment are demo assumptions and are labelled as such. Minoan Pulse is not a medical device.
